bridge: Builds on S05 channels and B03 sessions. This is a complete paper decision fixture using invented identities.
teaching:
Authentication establishes a principal; authorisation decides what that principal may do to a particular resource. A role can help express policy, but object ownership and context may still be required. Being signed in is not permission to read every record.

Model the decision as subject, action, object and conditions. Derive subject from a verified session and evaluate the current object state on the server. Deny by default when required information is absent. Client-side selectors are presentation controls, not the authority for assigning identity.

Sessions have a lifecycle: create after authentication, rotate when needed, expire and revoke. Least privilege limits capabilities to the job at hand. Revoking a session and deleting a local cookie are distinct actions; specify what a stolen copy can still do. Record both positive and negative permission cases so a blanket-deny implementation cannot appear correct.

ACLs attach permissions to objects and principals; capabilities carry unforgeable authority for particular objects/operations. They may be kernel-protected references or carefully scoped bearer tokens. Copying a token is not the same as proving a human identity, and delegated authority needs scope, expiry and any revocation mechanism. Mandatory access control means the policy constrains discretionary changes; it is broader than military secrecy levels. Strict Biba integrity and low-watermark variants are distinct policies. State the chosen rule before drawing an information-flow conclusion.

Authentication establishes a principal under an authenticator policy; authorisation checks what that principal may do to this object now. Two passwords are not two independent factor types. A possession authenticator with an activation factor may support multifactor authentication under its design, while phishing resistance requires additional properties such as binding authentication to the intended verifier. Recovery, new-authenticator enrolment and session theft must be considered alongside login. Evaluate accessibility and fallback paths for the actual users rather than assuming the older paper’s rankings apply unchanged. A per-password salt is public context for verification, not extra secret entropy.
example:
Policy fixture
A owns note1; B owns note2.
Readers may read their own notes.
Editors may update their own notes.
Admins may disable accounts but cannot read note bodies under this policy.
A: reader+editor; B: reader; C: admin

A read1 yes; A read2 no; B update2 no; C disableA yes; C read1 no.
explanation: The admin role is deliberately not universal. The policy demonstrates that role names alone do not define permissions; a decision must use the actual agreed rules. B's ownership does not grant update because B lacks the editor capability.
exercise: Evaluate A update1, A update2, B read2, B read1, C disableB, C read2 and an unauthenticated read1. Give the subject/action/object rule behind every answer.
solution: Answers: yes,no,yes,no,yes,no,no. Both role/capability and ownership matter. An absent session denies under this policy.
challenge: Add a suspended=true condition that blocks ordinary reads/updates but still allows admins to disable accounts. Evaluate suspended A read1 and C disableA. Explain where the suspension check belongs and how you would test session revocation.
challenge_solution: Suspended A is denied; C can disable A. Enforce current account state server-side rather than relying on a stale UI flag. Test a previously issued session after revocation and document the selected auth system's actual expiry/revocation semantics.
